## Open

### F-762 — A method named declare made lukaot unloadable by bare node, and tap hid it

> _2026-11-18 · core/lukaot · open_

`@feasibleone/lukaot` could not be loaded by bare `node` at all, and every test passed anyway.
`SignalRegistry` had a method named `declare`, and Node's type stripping refuses that name in a
class body: it strips the parameter types and then fails with
`SyntaxError: Unexpected identifier 'declare'` at the method. The whole package was therefore
unloadable in a real run — the framework executes TypeScript by stripping types, not by compiling it
— while `tap` ran the same files through swc and saw nothing wrong.

The symptom was indirect and cost three attempts to place: the framework's graceful-shutdown spawn
test began hanging, because the first framework class to hold the vocabulary was on the boot path
and the import threw where nobody was listening. A five-line probe
(`await import('@feasibleone/lukaot')` and a timer) reproduced it in a second and proved the import
held the boot graph, and a two-line file with one method named `declare` proved the cause.

Renamed to `declareSignal`. The lesson is not "avoid the word": it is that a package whose sources
are executed by Node's stripper is exercised only by a test runner that uses the same stripper, and
tap does not. Any `import` of a package from the framework's boot path needs one run under bare
`node` before it can be believed.

### F-770 — A declared-off capture could not be enabled by configuration

> _2026-11-20 · core/lukaot · open_

The framework's three captures were declared `enabled: false`, and a process that asked for them
with `log.capture.frameworkHttpExchange.enabled: true` recorded nothing at all.
`createCaptureSurface` skipped an entry whose declaration said `enabled: false` **before** calling
`resolve`, so the host that holds the configuration was never asked: the declaration was the last
word, and the operator's flag reached a member that had already returned. The silence was the
expensive part — a capture that does not run looks exactly like a capture whose rung is too cheap to
print anything.

The judgement moved to the resolver. The surface offers every entry and writes only what `resolve`
answers with; `LukaotLog.#resolveCapture` resolves `enabled` the way a log signal's is resolved, so
the configuration has the last word and the declaration is the default it starts from. The
lukaot-level test that pinned the old contract ("a disabled declaration writes nothing even when the
scope allows it") asserted the bug, and now pins the new one instead: the declaration reaches the
resolver, and a host that answers `undefined` builds nothing.
